title: Dominic Fike Talks ‘Rocket’ Mixtape, Fatherhood & ‘Babydoll’ Resurgence
contentText:
For years, the word “Rocket” has floated around Dominic Fike ’s mind. Long before it became the title of his latest project or even the name of his son, it was a word he kept returning to — attaching it to unfinished ideas, shelved projects, and future plans. Since breaking through in 2018 with Don’t Forget About Me, Demos under Columbia Records, the six-track EP led by breakout songs “3 Nights” and “Babydoll,” Fike became known as a genre-blurring artist whose effortless mix of soft rock, pop, hip-hop and rap made him one to watch.

Two years later came his debut album, What Could Possibly Go Wrong , an ambitious record that expanded his sound through tracks like “Vampire,” “Why,” and “Superstar Sh*t.” In 2023, Sunburn looked inward, with songs such as “Mama’s Boy” and “Mona Lisa” reflecting on home, family, and the Florida that shaped him. Throughout each era, “Rocket” surfaced repeatedly as a possible title, but never quite landed.

The idea dates back to one of the earliest chapters of Fike’s career: famously recording what would become his breakout extended play while on house arrest.

Born on Dec. 30, 1995, Fike grew up in Naples, Florida. He is of Filipino descent through his mother — a detail that has increasingly resonated with Filipino listeners as his career has grown internationally. Although Fike has previously shared that he wasn’t raised with a particularly strong connection to his Filipino heritage, his roots have nonetheless become a point of connection for many fans in the Philippines following his rise as both a musician and actor.

Throughout his career, Fike has spoken candidly about the instability that marked his upbringing, including both of his parents’ struggles with addiction. Even as his big break arrived, unpredictability continued to shape both his music and public persona. In 2017, after being charged with battery of a police officer during an incident involving his brother and subsequently being placed on house arrest, “Rocket” began to take on meaning. Thinking about its resemblance to shipping containers, he imagined rockets as vehicles of escape from his confinement.

When asked what made the word stay with him over the years, Fike describes it simply as, “I really like how it sounds and I like how it looks in my mind.”

For him, “Rocket” existed first as a feeling rather than a definition, a concept that resonated before it carried any concrete meaning. Years later, he would find an unexpected connection in Alan Watts’ The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are, which describes the rocket as one of America’s defining symbols of conquest.

“When I read that line, I felt like I made a good decision because I think I read that line after I named Rocket ,” Fike tells Billboard Philippines . While the passage didn’t give the word its meaning, it affirmed an idea that he had already believed in for years. For someone who had held onto the title through multiple projects, Rocket eventually came to symbolize Fike gaining control of where he was headed.

By the time the mixtape arrived in 2025, it had grown far beyond a working title and into a 12-track collection of beloved unreleased songs, fan favorites, and long-requested demos ahead of his next studio album.

Still, despite a career that spans two EPs, two studio albums, a mixtape, a breakout acting role in HBO’s Euphoria that introduced him to an even broader global audience, as well as collaborations with artists from Paul McCartney to JENNIE to Ravyn Lenae, Fike feels as if he’s always behind on releasing music. That ultimately became the driving force behind both Rocket and the eight-track EP 14 Minutes — a way of finally putting some of the hundreds of songs he’s accumulated into the world while fans await his full-length project.

“Even now, I’m having conversations with people about how I don’t release enough music,” Fike says, explaining what pushed him to release the songs now. More than simply having an overwhelming amount of material, he’s driven by the desire to make the kind of music he wants to hear, music that he feels doesn’t yet exist.

Rocket is filled with songs born from that mindset. Long before its official release, the project had become one fans eagerly anticipated, with snippets, unreleased tracks, and live previews circulating online for years, such as “One Glass,” “Sandman,” and “Epilogue.” They were songs Fike wanted out in the world for others to finally discover. With an entire online following built around his unfinished songs, even Fike laughs at the sheer amount of music he’s made that has never been released.

“I was talking to my homie Omar Apollo,” he says, “We were talking about the music we have in the vault, and he was like, ‘Yeah, dude, I have like 500 songs and I only like four of them.’ And I was like, ‘Dude, me too.’ Those four songs sometimes change, which means that there’s more than four songs.”

With what Fike calls “500 potential contestants” still sitting in the vault, Rocket represents the songs that ultimately made the cut after years of constant creation, revising, and refinement. In many ways, the mixtape’s arrival reflects the same journey as its title — arriving only when the time felt right.

Rocket may have spent years waiting for its release, but Fike has learned that songs often find listeners on their own timeline. Eight years after its own release, the Don’t Forget About Me, Demos track “Babydoll” unexpectedly found a second life, climbing streaming charts and introducing one of his earliest songs to an entirely new audience, even peaking at No. 34 at the Billboard Philippines Hot 100 chart.

“It’s really cool,” Fike says. “At first I was making an album in upstate New York when it happened, and it was just me and like five dudes… we were in a cabin in hoodies being like, ‘Oh shit,’ drinking coffee. The initial shock of it was very chill… and then I got to live out the reality of it happening, which was cool.”

For Fike, the unexpected resurgence of “Babydoll” served as another reminder that songs have a way of choosing their own moment. Rocket was no different. Though by the time of its release, “Rocket” had also taken on an entirely different meaning for Fike. In April 2026, he confirmed he had become a father to a son, Rocket, later sharing that parenthood had become one of the strongest motivations behind his sobriety and stability.

Extending well beyond his personal life, Fike says he’s also trying to become more intentional before opening the door to new collaborations.

While the people he works with regularly have grown accustomed to his creative habits, Fike confesses that anyone new to the process would probably find it “jarring.” For now, he means to focus on finding stability in his process, while still leaving the possibility open. “So no future collaborations right now until I’m musically stable, but shit, you never know.”

Beyond Rocket , Fike is also preparing to hit the road. He recently announced the North American leg of his Comedy Tragedy Parody Tour, which runs throughout August and September, following its Australian run that began in December 2025. The dates coincide with his guest appearances during Tame Impala’s Deadbeat Tour as the opening act starting Aug. 25 in Columbus, Ohio until Sept. 19 in Houston, Texas. Moving between the two spaces, Fike is in for a busy couple of months ahead.

Fatherhood, however, has inevitably changed what touring looks like. Fans have already caught glimpses of that new chapter, including when Fike brought Rocket onstage during his Lollapalooza performance. But, while playing in front of thousands of fans remains much the same, Fike says it’s everything that happens before and after the show that now feels different.

He further explains, “As far as touring goes, I mean, yeah, [fatherhood] makes touring a lot harder. I think that’s all it is. As far as schedules go and distance goes — I think it just makes it harder.”
